blocks.md: The easy cache asks which entry is oldest. This tier asks a harder question: **which data deserves the budget?** Values have different sizes, entries expire, and one cold scan can push out an entire hot working set.

blocks.caption: Pure LRU mistakes recent for reusable. A one-time scan looks important long enough to evict the data that will actually return.

blocks.title: Admission is a policy decision
blocks.md: Eviction chooses what leaves; admission chooses whether a new value should enter at all. Protecting hot residents from one-hit scan entries can matter more than finding a clever victim.

blocks.label: FIG 2
blocks.caption: Expiry is checked against virtual time. Reading does not extend life; replacing a value records a new expiry.

items: Charge `len(value) + contract.PerEntryMetadataBytes` for every resident entry.
Reject oversized inserts and replacements without evicting existing data.
Copy caller buffers and remove expired entries from both lookup and accounting.
The public workload requires a request hit rate of at least 40%; a cache that admits nothing does not pass.

items.title: Preserve the byte invariant
items.md: Handle replacement, expiry, and rejection before tuning policy.

items.title: Separate probation from protection
items.md: Give new entries a place to prove reuse before they can displace repeatedly used keys.

items.title: Measure the workload's cost
items.md: A miss on an expensive key matters more than a miss on a cheap one; compare byte hit rate with weighted backing cost.

blocks.title: A useful first improvement
blocks.md: A small probationary segment plus a protected segment is enough to make scan pollution visible in your design. You do not need a production cache algorithm before you can beat single-segment LRU.
